The petitioner has filed the present petition for seeking regular bail.

It has been asserted that the petitioner was arrested for the commission of offences punishable under Sections 20 and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (in short 'NDPS Act') vide FIR No. 188 of 2022, dated 5.12.2022, registered at Police Station Baijnath,

Yes. 
District Kangra, H.P.
As per the case of the prosecution, the petitioner was found in possession of 1.66 kgs charas.

However, .
the version of the police is absurd, baseless and based on imaginary stories.
The petitioner has no role in the commission of a crime.
There is no link evidence to connect the petitioner to the transportation of the contraband.
Co-accused Hemant Kumar admitted that he had cultivated the contraband and the bail petitioner had nothing to do with its cultivation.
The investigation is silent regarding the role attributed to the bail petitioner.
There is a violation of the standing order under Section 52A of the ND&PS Act.
There are reasonable grounds for believing that the petitioner had not committed any offence.
Previous cases are pending against the petitioner for the commission of offences punishable under the ND&PS Act, Section 376 of IPC and Sections 457 and 380 of IPC.
The petitioner was acquitted of the commission of an offence punishable under the ND&PS Act and no case is pending against him.
The petitioner is in judicial custody for the last one year and six months.
The prosecution has only examined five witnesses out of thirteen witnesses.
The prosecution has failed to complete the trial.

2. The police have filed a status report asserting that the police found a vehicle bearing registration no. HP-01K-4811 on 05.12.2022 at around 2:35 AM at Aberi.
The petitioner was found to be the driver of the vehicle.
Hemant Kumar was sitting in the rear seat of the vehicle.
The petitioner pushed a backpack towards the rear side after seeing the police.
Hemant Kumar tried to conceal the backpack.
The Police searched the backpack and found 1.66 kg of cannabis.
The police arrested the occupants and seized the contraband.
As per the report of SFSL, Junga, the substance was found to be of charas.
The contraband was disposed of by the Drug Disposal Committee on 24.2.2023.
The challan was prepared and presented before the Court.
Five witnesses have been examined out of 13 witnesses cited by the prosecution.

FIR no. 175 of 2009 dated 16.12.2009 was registered against the petitioner for the commission of offences punishable under Sections 376, 341 and 506 of IPC, in which the petitioner was convicted by the High Court on 16.08.2016.
FIR No.91 of 2012 dated 26.11.2012 was registered against the petitioner for the commission of offences punishable under Sections 20 and 29 of the NDPS Act, in which the petitioner was acquitted.

FIR No.202/2012 dated 29.12.2012 has been registered against the .
petitioner in Police Station Bhuntar, which is pending before the Court.

The petitioner was convicted by the Court in FIR no.101/2013 dated 10.10.2013 for the commission of offences punishable under Sections 363, 366, 376A and 506 of IPC and Section 4 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act.

sentences.text: The challan was presented before the learned Trial Court on 11.4.2023.
Five witnesses have been examined and eight witnesses are yet to be examined.
The matter is listed before the learned District & Sessions Judge, Dharamshala on 10.7.2024 and 11.7.2024.
3. I have heard Mr. Yashveer Singh Rathore, learned counsel for the petitioner and Mr. Lokender Kutlehria, learned Additional Advocate General for the respondent-State.
4. Mr. Yashveer Singh Rathore, learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the petitioner is innocent and he was falsely implicated.
The witnesses examined by the prosecution have not supported the prosecution case.
The testimonies of the witnesses were shattered in their cross-examination.

There is non compliance with the requirement of Section 52A of the ND&PS Act,
which is fatal to the prosecution case.

He relied .
upon the judgments of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in State of West Bengal Vs. Rakesh Singh 2022 SCC Online SC 828.

sentences.text: He further submitted that mere pendency of the criminal cases is no ground to deny bail.

5. Mr. Lokender Kutlehria, learned Additional Advocate General for the respondent-State submitted that there is no .
change in the circumstance.
The Court is not to appreciate the evidence at this stage.
The other submissions were already considered by the Court while rejecting the earlier bail application.

Hence,
he prayed that the present petition be dismissed.
6. I have given considerable thought to the submissions at the bar and have gone through the record carefully.

7. It is undisputed that the petitioner had earlier filed a bail petition bearing Cr.MP(M) No. 1992 of 2023, titled Ravinder Sharma Vs. State of H.P., decided on 22.12.2023 which was dismissed by this Court.

entities.text: Ravinder Sharma Vs. State of H.P.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was held in the State of Maharashtra Vs. Captain Buddhikota Subha Rao (1989) Suppl. 2 SCC 605 that once a bail application has been dismissed, subsequent bail application can only be considered if there is a change of circumstances.

entities.text: State of Maharashtra Vs. Captain Buddhikota Subha Rao (1989) Suppl. 2 SCC 605
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was observed:
"Once that application was rejected there was no question of granting a similar prayer.
That is virtually overruling the earlier decision without there being a change in the fact situation.
And when we speak of change, we mean a substantial one, which has a direct impact on the earlier decision and not merely cosmetic changes which are of little or no consequence.

'Between the two orders, there was a gap of only two days and it is nobody's case that during these .
two days, drastic changes had taken place necessitating the release of the respondent on bail.

Judicial discipline propriety and comity demanded that the impugned order should not have been passed reversing all earlier orders including the one rendered by Puranik, J. only a couple of days before, in the absence of any substantial change in the fact situation.

In such cases, it is necessary to act with restraint and circumspection so that the process of the Court is not abused by a litigant and an impression does not gain ground that the litigant has either successfully avoided one judge or selected another to secure an order which had hitherto eluded him.
8.

Similar is the judgment delivered in State of M.P. v.

sentences.text: It has further to be noted that the factum of the rejection of his earlier bail application bearing Miscellaneous Case No. 2052 of 2000 on 5-6-2000 has not been denied by the respondent.
It is true that successive bail applications are permissible under the changed circumstances.

But without the change in the circumstances, the second application would be deemed to be seeking a review of the earlier judgment which is not permissible under criminal law as has been held by this Court in Hari Singh Mann v. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa [(2001) 1 SCC 169: 2001 SCC (Cri) 113] and various other judgments.

entities.text: Hari Singh Mann v. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa [(2001) 1 SCC 169: 2001 SCC (Cri) 113]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 9. Similarly, it was held in Kalyan Chandra Sarkar Vs. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav (2004) 7 SCC 528 that where an earlier bail application has been rejected, the Court has to consider the rejection of the earlier bail application and then consider why the subsequent bail application should be allowed.

entities.text: Kalyan Chandra Sarkar Vs. Rajesh Ranjan @ Pappu Yadav (2004) 7 SCC 528
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was held:
.
"11.

In regard to cases where earlier bail applications have been rejected there is a further onus on the court to consider the subsequent application for grant of bail by noticing the grounds on which earlier bail applications have been rejected and after such consideration, if the court is of the opinion that bail has to be granted then the said court will have to give specific reasons why in spite of such earlier rejection the subsequent bail application should be granted."

10. A similar view was taken in State of T.N. v. S.A. Raja, (2005) 8 SCC 380, wherein it was observed:
9. When a learned Single Judge of the same court had denied bail to the respondent for certain reasons and that order was unsuccessfully challenged before the appellate forum, without there being any major change of circumstances, another fresh application should not have been dealt with within a short span of time unless there were valid grounds giving rise to a tenable case for bail.

entities.text: State of T.N. v. S.A. Raja, (2005) 8 SCC 380
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Of course, the principles of res judicata are not applicable to bail applications, but the repeated filing of bail applications without there being any change of circumstances would lead to bad precedents.

11. This position was reiterated in Prasad Shrikant Purohit v. State of Maharashtra, (2018) 11 SCC 458, wherein it was observed:
30.

entities.text: Prasad Shrikant Purohit v. State of Maharashtra, (2018) 11 SCC 458
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Before concluding, we must note that though an accused has a right to make successive applications for grant of bail, the court entertaining such subsequent bail Ravinder Sharma vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13193202/
4 applications has a duty to consider the reasons and grounds on which the earlier bail applications were rejected.

entities.text: Ravinder Sharma vs State Of Himachal Pradesh
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In such cases, the court also has a duty to record the fresh grounds which persuade it to take a view .
different from the one taken in the earlier applications.
12. Therefore, the present bail petition can only be considered on the basis of the change in the circumstances and it is not permissible to review the order passed by the Court.

The previous bail petition was denied on the ground that the petitioner was found in possession of 1.66 Kg. of charas,
which is a commercial quantity and the petitioner was unable to get out of the rigours of Section 37 of the ND&PS Act.
He had criminal antecedents which would not justify the grant of the bail to him.

Since the matter has already been considered; therefore, it is not permissible for the Court to say in the subsequent bail application that the petitioner was not found in possession of the commercial quantity of charas or that the bail can be granted to the petitioner despite his criminal antecedents.
13. The petitioner asserted that he is in judicial custody for one year and six months and the trial is likely to take a considerable time.
This cannot be accepted.
The status report shows that out of thirteen witnesses cited by the prosecution, five have been examined, eight are yet to be examined and the matter is now listed for 10.7.2024 and 11.7.2024.

The fact that the case has been listed for two consecutive dates shows the anxiety .
of the learned Trial Court to dispose of the matter at the earliest.
Hence, the petitioner cannot be granted bail on the ground of the delay.
14. Consequently, the present petition fails and the same is dismissed.
15. The observation made hereinabove shall remain confined to the disposal of the petition and will have no bearing, whatsoever, on the merits of the case.

(Rakesh Kainthla) Judge 14th June, 2024 (Chander)
